species.name: Pelidnota punctata
species.intro: For grapevine beetles I prepare two foods before introducing a pair. Adults feed mainly on the foliage of wild and cultivated grapes. Their young spend the winter inside decaying hardwood, where a newly hatched grub can begin tunneling as soon as it leaves the egg.

sections.title: Adult food and pairing
sections.text:
I would give the adults fresh grape cuttings with enough foliage to perch on while feeding. They also eat the grapes themselves and sometimes feed on Virginia creeper. During the day they often rest on the host plant. After dark they fly, come to lights and pair on the vines, so evening is a good time to check for mating. The arrangement of spots can look quite different between beetles. Northern adults tend to have dark legs and conspicuous markings, while Florida and Texas adults can have pale legs and almost no spots. I would keep the locality with each pair.
I photographed the reddish form from Key Largo, Florida, in June. That beetle had almost no visible spotting on its back. Its color is a good example of why I keep the locality with my stock.

sections.title: The laying site and eggs
sections.text: For a laying site I recommend placing moist soil against soft, decomposing hardwood. In the field, females lay singly in the soil beneath rotten logs or beside decaying stumps. Sometimes a female encloses an egg in a small ball of earth, which breaks easily when the surrounding soil is disturbed. I would leave the soil and wood together through hatching. The short distance to food matters here because a new grub can immediately bore into the adjacent wood.

sections.title: Larval food and emergence
sections.text:
I would use lightly fermented hardwood flake soil for the grubs and include a piece of well-decayed hardwood. In nature the larvae feed in old logs and stumps or tunnel along their decaying roots. Elm, walnut, cherry and birch are among their recorded hardwoods. For timing I use a field-based estimate from Lexington, Kentucky, where larvae overwintered and the life cycle appeared to take about two years. That is a regional benchmark for planning how long to keep a brood. I would record the hatching and emergence dates for each locality before settling on a timetable for my own stock.
I have kept grapevine beetles using the same general arrangement I use for Dynastes and have reared them to the pupal stage. I leave a formed chamber intact while the adult develops inside.
When setting up feeding grubs, I also use my Chrysina woodi guide as a reference for choosing lightly fermented hardwood material. For grapevine beetles I include decayed wood; my own captive pupa and the wood occupied by wild grubs are my reference points for this species.

species.name: Odontotaenius disjunctus
species.intro: In my compacted raw-sawdust setup, the horned passalus adults stayed alive, but I did not get a brood. That result changed what I would look for in a breeding enclosure. I want a piece of moist, well-decayed hardwood large enough to hold an intact family and its galleries.

sections.title: Setting up occupied wood
sections.text: For a breeding attempt I recommend starting with a section of the log the beetles already occupy. I look for decayed hardwood soft enough for feeding but firm enough that the gallery walls stay intact. I would preserve the material inside those galleries as well as the beetles themselves. My sawdust trial was useful for keeping adults alive. It did not give me a reason to substitute compacted sawdust for an occupied log when my goal is reproduction.

sections.title: Keeping the family together
sections.text: I treat a passalus gallery differently from a jar of solitary stag beetle larvae. Here, adults and young occupy the same wood. The parents chew wood, accumulate frass and prepare food that the larvae can eat. I recommend leaving the fine material along the walls in place when adding a fresh piece of softened wood. If I find eggs or young, I keep the occupied section with its adults instead of transferring each grub to a clean cup.

sections.title: Pupal chambers and young adults
sections.text: I avoid splitting a section of wood that contains a brood to look for pupae. Adults build and repair chambers around the pupae, and older siblings can help maintain them. A newly emerged adult can be reddish before its cuticle darkens. I would leave it with the family, especially when there are still younger larvae and intact chambers in the same log. For this species my own trial establishes what supported adult survival. I have yet to obtain offspring in compacted raw sawdust.

species.name: Tenebrio molitor
species.intro: A mealworm colony is easiest to follow when I can tell which tray holds the laying adults, which holds the feeding larvae and which is waiting on new beetles. For a small colony I recommend dry wheat bran and a separate piece of carrot or potato for moisture. The grain itself is food for both the adults and their young.

sections.title: Preparing a laying tray
sections.text: I recommend a shallow, ventilated container with a layer of dry wheat bran. I place the moisture food where it is easy to remove, and replace it before it softens or develops mold. A small fresh piece is easier to manage than a large slice left in the grain. I want the bran around the beetles to stay loose and dry. I would date the box when the adults go in, especially if I plan to run more than one brood.

sections.title: Recovering young larvae
sections.text: When the adults have had time to lay, I recommend transferring the beetles to a fresh tray and keeping the old bran. The eggs are small enough to miss, and the first larvae are much less conspicuous than the familiar yellow mealworms. Keeping the laying substrate gives them time to hatch and start feeding. As they grow, I would add fresh bran and keep the same small moisture source available.

sections.title: Saving pupae for the next generation
sections.text: To keep a colony going, I leave a portion of the larger mealworms to mature. I separate the pale, soft pupae from active feeding larvae and keep them where I can check for emergence. A newly emerged beetle is pale and gradually darkens as its cuticle hardens. Once the beetles are active, I recommend giving them fresh bran in a dated laying tray. When generations overlap, that simple separation makes it much easier to follow a new batch without discarding the eggs with spent grain.

species.name: Gymnetis thula
species.intro: I reared a group of harlequin flower beetles on used aspen shavings from a snake enclosure mixed with sand. Every larva survived and the adults were average-sized. I use the photographs below to show what the mix looked like.

sections.title: Feeding the adults
sections.text: For active adults, my usual food is beetle jelly. I replace it about every five days. Pieces of banana or apple also work as adult food. I keep the feeding spot accessible at the surface so I can change the food without disturbing the substrate below. In the wild, adults visit flowers and sap flows. In Texas they have been observed at sap on false willow. These beetles take flight readily, especially when disturbed, so check the lid for adults as you open the enclosure.

sections.title: Setting up for eggs and larvae
sections.text: In my aspen trial I used bedding that had already been used in a snake enclosure. I mixed the shavings with sand and kept the grubs in that mixture through development. If I use a different substrate, I look for decaying plant matter. In the field females lay in compost or fermenting oak, and the grubs also occupy organic matter inside tree hollows. I check the bedding below the surface when judging moisture.

sections.title: Pupal cells and new adults
sections.text: The white, curved grubs pass through three instars and can reach roughly 25 mm. A mature larva builds an oval chamber for pupation. When working through older substrate, look for intact cells before breaking up lumps or throwing out material. I recommend leaving each cell supported on all sides until its occupant emerges. Supply beetle jelly again when the adults become active. The cream pattern on the head, thorax and wing covers varies considerably among beetles of this species.

species.name: Dynastes tityus
species.intro: I have raised hundreds of eastern Hercules beetles in Michigan. I can rear a large brood on organic raised-bed soil, and I have also raised sizeable males on used substrate. A newly formed adult may sit through the winter in its pupal chamber, so I plan the next pairing around when the beetles actually come up and feed.

sections.title: Feeding and pairing active adults
sections.text:
I keep an active male and female together. I offer beetle jelly every five days, or a piece of apple or banana. I watch for the female to feed and burrow before checking for eggs. I prefer to see a mating when I can. In my experience, roughly a third of the wild-caught females I have worked with appeared to be unmated. A female from the Texas Sandhills was one of them.
Season matters when putting a pair together. Adults I collected in northern Florida in 2024 became active in late May the following year. I wait for both beetles to be active before pairing them.
In North Carolina I found seven adults in a single night. The largest male there was over 63 mm by my field measurement. In a comparison of three males from my collection, the intermediate one measured around 55 mm.

sections.title: Choosing substrate for a large brood
sections.text:
When I was raising hundreds at once, I used a locally available organic raised-bed soil as a cheaper alternative to flake soil. It worked for my Michigan colony, although I had to change it more often. Products sold as raised-bed soil vary from place to place. Before using a whole bag for a brood, I would try a small batch and follow how well the grubs feed and grow. The major males I raised this way measured about 55–62 mm. I never reached 65 mm with that method.
I have also obtained males over 55 mm on spent substrate that the larvae had reduced almost entirely to dry frass. That was a separate trial. If I use hardwood flake soil for a new brood, I choose a more thoroughly fermented batch than I would for stag beetles and replace it as the grubs consume it.

sections.title: Wood in the field and in culture
sections.text:
Tree cavities are a good place to look for the loose material the larvae eat. I have seen this species use standing dead pine. In 2021 I kept an Alabama line that came from pine and had been raised on potting soil. I keep that distinction in mind when choosing a substrate. The material a grub came from in the woods and the food it developed on afterward can be quite different.
In Wetumpka, Alabama, I found one of my males as a second-instar grub in a decayed pine in January 2012. In a separate January search I found 14 larvae in the cavity of a fallen tree in a suburban area. I look at the condition of the material inside a cavity when judging whether it can support grubs.

sections.title: Pupal chambers and overwintering
sections.text: Once a grub finishes shaping its chamber, I leave it intact. On three separate occasions I found wild adults still inside their chambers, in October, November and April. I allow about two to three years for larval development in the wild. Inside a clear container, I can follow a chamber at the wall without opening it. I begin offering food once the adult leaves the chamber and comes to the surface.

species.name: Lucanus elaphus
species.intro: I started my giant stag beetle line with wild adults from North Carolina. They produced a brood that fall, and I reared those larvae to adulthood. Getting their offspring to breed took another season. I gave the captive-bred adults a long cool rest, then obtained eggs that hatched into my second generation.

sections.title: Setting up the adults
sections.text:
Females I collected at Auburn, Alabama, helped me work out how dry to keep the laying box. I had tried logs, ordinary flake soil and potting soil with little success. When I offered these females much drier sawdust, about as dry as I use for my longhorn beetles, they laid readily and I recovered enough larvae for another generation. My L. placidus and L. capreolus laid well in my usual flake soil.
For active adults I offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana. A piece of bark on the surface gives the adults footing. Once the female buries herself, I leave her time to lay. In the wild, the larvae have also been found in decaying logs and underneath them at the wood–soil interface.

sections.title: Rearing larvae and checking for cells
sections.text:
When I check a laying box, I lift each piece of wood over the container so that loose substrate and any grubs stay together. Keep enough of the original feeding wood with the brood to avoid losing larvae still inside it. This is a long-lived grub. Ulyshen and colleagues estimated one to two years for development, and 16 males in their study waited an additional year to pupate. Look against the bottom of a clear container for pupal cells before replacing food. Among individuals that pupated within a year of collection, females spent about 29 days as pupae and males about 31.
I have seen quite different schedules at different temperatures. At ordinary room temperature, one group stayed in its cells for about two years before emerging. One of the males was about 55 mm long. In a separate laboratory group kept around 78–80 °F (26–27 °C), the larvae pupated within nine months. I record cell construction, pupation and adult emergence separately when I follow a brood.

sections.title: Overwintering the next generation
sections.text: I once had larvae that remained at the same stage for months. After a faulty air conditioner kept the room unusually cool for several July days, my stalled grubs became prepupae. For the adults of my North Carolina line I gave them eight months in a wine cooler at 55 °F (about 13 °C). The adults then laid eggs over the following two months. Once I could see young grubs again, I knew I had carried the line through another generation.

species.name: Chrysina woodi
species.intro: The first thing I notice about a live Chrysina woodi is the contrast between its emerald-green back and its metallic blue feet. I bred this scarab from West Texas adults. A pair needs fresh foliage throughout the laying period, and a mature grub needs a place to build its pupal cell below its food.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: 1.5–3 years in the seasonally cooled culture. My West Texas stock reached adulthood in about six months.

facts.title: Egg count
facts.text: 20–60 or more in the seasonal culture. One West Texas female laid 122 eggs.

sections.title: Choosing and feeding the adults
sections.text: I start with fresh hickory foliage. My West Texas adults fed on it readily. Walnut works too, and pecan is a convenient alternative in the eastern United States. I keep spare cuttings in a closed bag in the refrigerator for up to a week and give the beetles fresh branches every three days. In the field, adults fly along mountain arroyos on cloudy days and at night, particularly in humid summer weather. To sex a pair, I check the underside of the abdomen. A female has a fine line down the middle of the terminal segment. A male has a dark segment that is absent in females. Adults measure about 25–35 mm.

sections.title: Setting up a laying enclosure
sections.text: For a laying enclosure, I use a medium-size, well-ventilated Critter Keeper or larger, with a capacity of at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). I add 3 inches (7.5 cm) of loose, lightly fermented hardwood flake soil. A handful should hold together when squeezed without releasing any water. I leave the soil uncompacted. A female may spend several days feeding, disappear below the surface to lay, then return to the branches. I leave the eggs in place because the adults leave them unharmed. I usually allow for 20–60 eggs or more and one to three months of adult life. I rate this species 8 out of 10 for breeding difficulty.

sections.title: Larval food, winter cooling and pupation
sections.text:
I rear the grubs individually on lightly fermented hardwood flake soil. Decayed hardwood also serves as larval food. For a brood that reaches the late third instar in the fall, I put about 2 inches (5 cm) of clay or similarly textured pupation soil beneath the feeding layer. I keep the larvae in the low 40s to 50s °F (roughly 5–15 °C) through winter and warm them in spring. When I skipped cooling, some larvae failed to pupate and some adults emerged too far apart to pair. Adults surface on their own a few months after warming. I let new females feed away from males for several days before pairing them. In this seasonal setup, larval development took 1½–3 years and pupation about a month. My West Texas trial developed much faster.
In spring 2020, three of my adults emerged over the course of several weeks. I have the food plant ready before the first beetle surfaces so I can start feeding it while I wait for the others.

species.name: Xyloryctes thestalus
species.intro: After three years of trying to breed the western rhinoceros beetle, I finally reared adults from eggs laid in captivity. The surprise was the timing. My adults produced just one egg before winter. Most of the breeding happened the following spring, after beetles that had spent months underground returned to the surface and began feeding again.

sections.title: Setting up and feeding the adults
sections.text: I used a well-ventilated enclosure with 4–5 in (10–13 cm) of lightly fermented flake soil and pieces of bark across the surface. I kept the flake soil slightly moist, around the moisture level I use for stag beetles and a little drier than I ordinarily use for rhinoceros beetles. The adults showed a clear preference for apple and other firm fruits over softer foods.

sections.title: Overwintering and spring egg laying
sections.text:
By late October the adults had buried themselves and stopped eating. I kept the enclosure at about 68–75 °F (20–24 °C) throughout the winter. They stayed below the surface until April. When they came back up, they fed again and breeding activity increased. The single egg laid before winter eventually produced a male. All the other eggs and larvae I recovered came from April through July. On June 30, 2023, I found both fresh eggs and young grubs in the enclosure of my Fort Davis, Texas stock.
I would keep an apparently unproductive autumn setup through the following spring. Some of the wild adults I collected on August 5, 2022, were still alive more than a year later. Their ability to resume feeding and breeding after such a long interval underground made it worth keeping the colony together.

sections.title: Choosing flake soil for the next generation
sections.text: I keep the laying and larval substrates separate in my notes. The 4–5 inches of lightly fermented flake soil and the slightly drier surface were the conditions in which my adults laid. For a separate larval container, my usual starting point for rhinoceros beetles is a more thoroughly fermented hardwood flake soil. I follow each larva’s feeding and leave a formed pupal chamber intact. The result that mattered most in this culture was finding eggs and larvae again in spring after the long winter pause.

species.name: Strategus aloeus
species.intro: One of the males I bred measured 53 mm. For such a substantial beetle, the ox beetle has a surprisingly short larval period and a long adult life. My larvae reached adulthood in less than a year on organic raised-bed soil. Once the adults were active, keeping up with their appetite took more attention than preparing the breeding substrate.

sections.title: Adult care and laying
sections.text: My adults ate heavily, so I supplied fresh food every three days. Beetle jelly, apple and banana are my usual choices for fruit-feeding adults. Adult males can live as long as two years. The longest-lived female in my own colony survived about nine months. My females accepted several organic substrates for laying, so I was able to use a simple setup. In one July laying box I could see eggs from a wild-caught female through the clear wall. One male I had photographed as a pupa in January 2022 was still alive and well the following January.

sections.title: Feeding the grubs and building a pupal cell
sections.text:
I have reared grubs to adulthood on organic raised-bed soil and on flake soil. For growing rhinoceros beetle larvae, I choose thoroughly fermented hardwood flake soil. As they approach full size, I give every Strategus species I rear a firmly packed layer of clay-like soil for pupation. I put the clay beneath the feeding substrate, where the grub can reach it and shape a chamber that holds together. This is the same arrangement I use for my Chrysina. Once I see the outline of a pupal cell, I leave the soil around it in place until the adult emerges. In an earlier raised-bed-soil trial, adults also emerged without my adding a separate layer of topsoil.
I have seen full-grown grubs walk repeatedly across the surface looking for a place to settle. In my culture they stopped wandering when I moved them onto clay that held together under pressure. Surface wandering at this stage is my cue to check that the pupation layer is accessible.

sections.title: Developmental timing in a published colony
sections.text: Ahumada and colleagues measured each stage in beetles from Puerto Wilches, Colombia, reared at 29–32 °C. Eggs averaged about 15 days to hatch. Of the three larval instars, the first averaged 24 days, the second 42 days and the third about 201 days. Pupation averaged another 27 days, bringing the egg-to-adult interval to about 308 days. That long final instar accounts for much of the wait after a grub has become conspicuously large. For comparison, my own larvae completed development in raised-bed soil in less than a year.

sections.title: Keeping eastern and western stocks separate
sections.text: I keep locality labels with each line and pair beetles from the same regional stock. I treat the eastern and western populations as two putative species within the Strategus aloeus complex. I group Arizona and New Mexico with the western stock, and western Texas eastward with the eastern stock. I cannot assign my 2022 captive series to either group from its locality data.

species.name: Mallodon dasystomus
species.intro: A large hardwood stump borer can approach 5 cm in length. I consider it a good first longhorn to rear because the females accept a simple bed of damp sawdust and the larvae feed on hardwood pellets after they have been expanded into sawdust. The main commitment is time. The larvae can spend several years feeding before they mature.

sections.title: Pairing and preparing the laying box
sections.text:
I keep this hardwood stump borer and Stenodontes chevrolati, and the difference in build is especially apparent when I have males of both side by side. A major male Mallodon has a broad head and substantial mandibles. When I introduce the adults I stay nearby to watch them together. For the female, the most useful feature of my setup is how little material the laying box needs. I can provide the egg-laying surface with hardwood sawdust alone.
When both sexes are available, I also compare the pronotum, the shield just behind the head. In my males it looks rectangular from above. In females the outline is rounder. This gives me a second feature to check alongside the head and mandibles.

sections.title: Finding the eggs
sections.text: I spread about half an inch (1.3 cm) of damp hardwood sawdust in the laying container. My females laid in that shallow layer without an intact log. When I check the substrate, I look carefully at any particle that resembles a seed. The eggs are surprisingly hard-shelled and easy to overlook among coarse pieces of wood. The half-inch depth is what I use to find eggs in the female’s box. I set up the feeding larvae separately with their own supply of wood.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae
sections.text: I start with plain hardwood pellets and expand them into sawdust. The larvae eat the wood itself, so I treat it as their food supply when I check the container. Kinshi, hardwood sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium, is another larval food this species will accept. My larvae also accepted supplementary protein and grew rapidly when it was available. I can rear them on hardwood sawdust without having to supply a whole stump.

sections.title: Allowing time for development
sections.text: I allow about one to three years for the larval stage, depending on the rearing conditions. A small grub with fresh sawdust still available and a nearly full-grown one that has consumed most of its food need attention at different times. I check what remains in each container before deciding when to replenish it. I keep the food type with the date I set up each larva so I can compare growth within the same brood.

species.name: Stenodontes chevrolati
species.intro: Stenodontes chevrolati is a large prionine longhorn native to southern Florida and parts of the Caribbean. I used to see it only rarely in collections. Captive breeding has made it easier to obtain, and I find it fairly straightforward to rear once I have an active pair. The step I pay closest attention to is separating the young larvae as soon as they hatch.

facts.title: Larval period
facts.text: Usually 1–3 years overall. About 8 months on kinshi in my fastest cultures.

sections.title: Pairing the adults
sections.text: I have never seen my adults feed. They appear to live on reserves accumulated as larvae, and some of mine have lived as long as four months. Once both beetles are active, I introduce the male to the female and watch for mating. My pairs usually mate almost immediately. One mating seems sufficient for the female to lay fertile eggs for the rest of her life. I remove the male afterward because he will keep trying to mate while she is trying to lay.

sections.title: Egg laying and the first galleries
sections.text: For one mated female, I pack raw hardwood sawdust into a container of at least 32 US fl oz (about 0.95 L) and lay a paper towel over the surface. She deposits her eggs on or just below the surface of the sawdust. I expect them to hatch in about a month. The first sign I look for is a set of tiny galleries against the container wall. As soon as I see them, I take the laying box apart and gently sift through the sawdust. I move each hatchling to its own container because the larvae readily cannibalize one another.

sections.title: Choosing a larval substrate
sections.text:
I give each larva a container of at least 32 fl oz and prefer a one-gallon jar (3.8 L). I use raw hardwood sawdust, lightly fermented sawdust that has gone through one fermentation, or kinshi, which is sawdust colonized by fungal mycelium. My larvae grew fastest on kinshi, followed by lightly fermented sawdust. On raw sawdust they took about 18–24 months to mature. On kinshi they could reach the same stage in about eight months.
I have also collected larvae in the Florida Keys. For following the growth of those wood-boring grubs in captivity, an individual clear-sided jar lets me see the tunnels without opening the substrate each time.

sections.title: Changing food and recognizing pupation
sections.text: With kinshi, I look through the sides of the bottle. When I can no longer see fungus-colonized substrate at the wall, I move the larva to a fresh bottle. With raw or lightly fermented sawdust, I can usually leave the jar for six to eight months between changes. A full-grown larva builds a pupal cell and may spend several months inside. The pupal stage itself lasts about a month. I leave the cell intact and wait for the new adults to become active before introducing another pair.

sections.title: Male size in culture
sections.text: The male I photographed in February 2024 measured about 75 mm. My largest male measured 78 mm. I have kept this species alongside Mallodon dasystomus, another prionine I breed. Even an average male Mallodon can look small when the two are side by side.

species.name: Dynastes grantii
species.intro: With western Hercules beetles, I prepare more than one laying box before I pair the adults. A single female can produce a large number of eggs, and the grubs from one brood can reach pupation weeks apart. I keep the laying date with each box so I can follow the brood even after I move the adults.

sections.title: Offering food and pairing the adults
sections.text: I offer active adults beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana. I let a newly emerged beetle come up and start feeding before I introduce a mate. I keep the pair where I can see both beetles on the surface, with enough substrate below for the female to burrow. Once I have seen them pair, I can move the female to her own laying box. I like a clear-sided box because I can sometimes see eggs or a pupa without digging.

sections.title: Eggs and the feeding substrate
sections.text:
One female gave me 87 eggs. In a different box that originally held more than 80 eggs, I later found just 12 living larvae. I keep those counts separate when planning how many rearing containers I need. A large egg count tells me how much space to prepare, but the number of feeding grubs can be quite different.
For growing rhinoceros beetle larvae I recommend thoroughly fermented hardwood flake soil. I use a more fermented batch than I would for stag beetles or jewel scarabs. I check the substrate while the larva is still feeding so I can replace exhausted food before it begins making a cell.

sections.title: Prepupae, pupae and emergence
sections.text:
In one brood, a single grub reached the prepupal stage long before its siblings. In a display enclosure I could see a larva starting its pupal cell on September 23 and a pupa at the wall on October 17. I keep the cell intact and continue checking the slower grubs separately. When a chamber is visible through the side, I can follow the stages without lifting it out. I wait until a new adult comes out on its own and is feeding before I pair it.
In one earlier pair the male had already emerged while the female was still a pupa. She completed her adult molt the day I photographed the male. I keep each chamber intact even if its occupant appears to be behind the rest of the group.

sections.title: Adult lifespan
sections.text: When planning for older adults, I keep in mind an unusually long-lived Arizona male documented by Krell and Krell. It survived nine months and one week after collection. That is a useful upper-end comparison when an active western Hercules beetle lives well beyond the breeding season.

species.name: Euphoria monticola
species.intro: I started my Euphoria monticola culture with several grubs I found beneath decomposing leaves in Arizona. They are difficult to find in the wild. The adults fly in the canopy and visit sap flows, so they can be easy to miss from the ground. I raised my larvae to adults and obtained one captive generation. I rate the species 6 out of 10 for difficulty.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Adults and egg laying
sections.text: These southwestern flower chafers occur in Arizona and New Mexico and range south into Mexico. Adults measure about 10–15 mm. The two beetles pictured here give a sense of the color variation, one metallic green and the other blue-black. Mine readily accepted fruit and beetle jelly and lived about one to three months. I recommend a breeding container that holds at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). Offer the adult food at the surface and give females flake soil or an organic substrate of decaying hardwood and well-decomposed leaves in which to lay. They can produce 30 or more eggs.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae
sections.text: The hatchlings can start feeding in the same material their mother laid in. I allow about 18 months for the larval stage, so keep enough of the same food on hand for substrate changes. I lost the next generation after moving the young grubs to potting soil. I can’t say exactly what caused the loss. For another brood I’d keep the grubs on flake soil or replenish the mixture of decayed wood and leaves that supported them earlier.

sections.title: Autumn cocoons and spring emergence
sections.text: The hardest part for me was getting the mature larvae through winter. All of them built cocoons in autumn, then spent several months inside as larvae. Only after I moved the cocoons into a cold garage for winter did the larvae become prepupae. They pupated when the weather warmed in spring, and adults appeared within about a month. I have no measured garage temperature to recommend, and the length of pupation and dormancy varies. If you are following a brood of your own, note when a cell first appears and leave it in place. The larva may spend a season inside before it actually pupates.

species.name: Osmoderma eremicola
species.intro: I give this eastern hermit beetle about two years, sometimes longer, to finish its larval development. Even the second-instar grubs can make chambers and stay inside for weeks. Mine came back out to feed, then molted again before their final winter rest. Despite the long life cycle, I rate the species 3 out of 10 for difficulty.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Adults and breeding substrate
sections.text: Adults measure roughly 25–30 mm and live for about one to three months. They fly in the canopy and visit sap flows in the wild. I recommend a breeding container of at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). In captivity I offer fruit or beetle jelly when they become active. Even unfed females laid eggs for me, but they lived for less time and produced fewer eggs than females with access to food. Egg counts can reach 30 or more. To select a pair, look at the head and the plate directly behind it, the pronotum. Steffek and colleagues used the conspicuous depressions in both structures to recognize males.

sections.title: Feeding grubs and temporary chambers
sections.text:
The grubs live in pockets of decayed hardwood inside tree cavities. One Wisconsin beetle was reared from rotting silver maple. I use flake soil, decayed wood, or a mixture with thoroughly decomposed hardwood leaves. Once the grubs have reduced their food to a pile of frass, give them fresh substrate. In summer or autumn my second instars made small chambers and remained inside for several weeks, sometimes a month. Leave these chambers alone. The grubs came back out, resumed feeding and quickly reached the third instar. They overwintered as third instars and reached full size by the end of the following year.
I once accidentally broke the same larva’s chamber three times. It rebuilt each time and pupated in its fourth chamber. By the third attempt it was down to about two-thirds of its earlier size. The damp material held together like clay. Seeing the larva lose that much bulk is why I leave an intact cell supported by the surrounding substrate.

sections.title: Overwintering mature larvae
sections.text: Once my third instars were fully grown, I moved them into a garage for about three months. Winter temperatures there were in the low 50s °F (roughly 10–12 °C). Overlapping emergence matters because the adults are relatively short-lived. The pupal stage lasts about a month, and the dormancy period is roughly three weeks. I leave each cell supported by its surrounding substrate. The wall can break simply from lifting it. When the adults emerge, move them into a fresh breeding bin and provide food for the next pairing.

species.name: Chrysina gloriosa
species.intro: I set up my glorious jewel scarabs for breeding as soon as I have active adults. Their one to three months above ground leave little time to spare. Getting eggs is only the beginning. I rate this species 8 out of 10 for difficulty because maintaining it through successive generations has proved much harder.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: Arizona, New Mexico and western Texas

sections.title: Sexing and feeding a pair
sections.text: My adults measure about 20–30 mm. Males tend to be smaller, but I check the underside of the abdomen when choosing a pair. In a female, the last abdominal segment has a pointed, V-shaped outline. In a male, it is more rounded or U-shaped, with a narrow slit visible at the tip. I provide juniper cuttings in a breeding bin of at least 1.75 US gallons (6.6 L). Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) works well. I change the cuttings every three days and keep old foliage out of the bin. My adults have been prone to fungal and bacterial problems when cuttings are left to deteriorate. I have also found adults flying at night in August even under extremely dry field conditions.

sections.title: Recognizing the laying cycle
sections.text: I leave the eggs where the female lays them. A female typically spends several days feeding on the juniper, burrows for about a day, then comes up to feed again. This cycle can repeat several times. I keep the foliage fresh even when the beetles are below ground. I expect roughly 20–60 eggs, sometimes more. My adults have left the eggs alone, and the grubs can hatch directly into the shared substrate. In one season I photographed eggs on May 31 and had second-generation hatchlings by June 4. Those were dates for the culture as a whole. The following July I had third-generation offspring.

sections.title: Feeding the grubs
sections.text: I raise the grubs on lightly fermented hardwood flake soil. In the wild, the larvae also use decaying hardwood. In southeastern Arizona, for example, they have been found in rotting Arizona sycamore (Platanus wrightii). The juniper I give the parents belongs above ground as fresh foliage. The young need the decomposing wood below. My larvae generally reach the latter part of their third and final instar by autumn. I allow 1½–3 years for the larval stage and about a month for the pupa.

sections.title: Overwintering and pairing the next generation
sections.text: I keep late third instars cool through the winter, from the low 40s into the 50s °F (roughly 5–15 °C). When I skipped winter cooling, larvae often failed to pupate, or adults emerged so far apart that I could not pair them. I warm the containers in spring and wait. The adults come to the surface on their own after a few months. I keep a newly surfaced female away from males for the first several days and give her fresh juniper to feed on. Persistent mating attempts at this vulnerable stage can kill her.

species.name: Osmoderma subplanatum
species.intro: My Osmoderma subplanatum larvae grew quickly on flake soil from Georgia Beetle Supplies. When I checked them in June, they were already third instars. A month earlier they had been first instars. For a new brood, that gives me a practical starting substrate and a reason to check early growth sooner than I might expect for a hermit beetle.

facts.title: First to third instar
facts.text: About one month from first to third instar

sections.title: Feeding young grubs
sections.text:
I started with ten larvae one year and had adults breeding by June 8 the following year. In a second growth check, grubs that had been first instars a month earlier were already third instars. I keep prepared hardwood flake soil on hand as they consume it. If I use natural material, I choose well-decayed hardwood. In Nebraska, one standing ash contained about 45 third instars. Grubs have also been found in rotting maple and boxelder.
For the rest of the breeding setup I use my Osmoderma eremicola method. I keep softened wood mixed into the feeding substrate and leave closed cells intact. I follow the stages of the subplanatum brood itself when deciding when to look for adults.

sections.title: Timing the final instar
sections.text: I would allow plenty of time after the first two molts. Ratcliffe followed Nebraska grubs collected as third instars in July. He recorded both pupae and adults in February, but four beetles were still larvae the following June. Survival was poor in that group. Those dates give a sense of how much individuals can differ even when they start at the same instar. A brood reaching the third instar in a month can still be months from adulthood.

sections.title: Pupation and identification
sections.text: Pupae described from Nebraska measured 30–36 mm. They were pale at first and darkened toward brown before the adult molt. Keep the collection locality and parentage with each container until emergence. Third instars of this species and Osmoderma eremicola are difficult to separate even under magnification. An adult associated with the brood gives you much better grounds for confirming the identification. Older publications treat this beetle under the spelling Osmoderma subplanata. I found pupal cells in my culture in late October. Some adults I reared lacked red spots, and some of my O. eremicola had them. I keep the species and locality label with each brood because spotting alone has proved unreliable.

species.name: Osmoderma scabrum
species.intro: My rough hermit beetles were in dormancy cells in late January. When I find one of those occupied chambers, I leave it supported by the surrounding substrate. The larva uses pieces of the material it has lived in to build the chamber wall, so an ordinary-looking clump can hold a resting beetle.

facts.title: Adult feeding in our collection
facts.text: Offer beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana.

sections.title: Choosing larval food
sections.text: I have seen adults feeding at sap flows in the wild. For a larval enclosure I recommend soft, decayed hardwood with enough texture left for cell construction. William Saunders recorded the white, reddish-headed grubs in rotten portions of apple and cherry trees. A tree can still be alive and have a pocket of suitable decay inside it. The grubs feed within that softened wood. Saunders described mature larvae gathering fragments and binding them together into oval cells in autumn.

sections.title: Recognizing dormancy
sections.text: I photographed my beetles in their cells on January 24, 2026. A completed chamber can contain a resting larva before pupation, and I leave the occupant undisturbed through this interval. If you uncover the wall while renewing food elsewhere in the enclosure, keep the material immediately around it in place. Date the first visible cell separately from the day an adult appears at the surface.

sections.title: Watching the adults
sections.text: In field observations, adults sheltered during the day and visited sap after dark. Saunders found them active in July. For a captive group, I recommend checking the surface in the evening and waiting until the beetles have left their cells before selecting a pair. The wing covers are distinctly rough, a useful feature for distinguishing them from the smoother Osmoderma eremicola. Males can be recognized by conspicuous depressions on the head and pronotum. Older literature uses the spelling Osmoderma scabra.

species.name: Lucanus mazama
species.intro: I have had good adult emergence with the cottonwood stag beetle, sometimes with a whole group of beetles coming up together. Some of my males were noticeably larger than others. This is a productive species on hardwood flake soil. A single female gave me 46 larvae when I opened her laying box.

sections.title: Pairing and egg laying
sections.text: The male’s inward-curving mandibles are larger than the female’s. I set up the laying substrate before introducing an active pair. I use aged hardwood sawdust with this species, and it has bred on flake soil. For a new box I recommend the less-fermented hardwood mix described on the Substrate page. My longstanding flake recipe uses sawdust, flour, yeast and a little oatmeal, stirred over one to two months. Offer active adults beetle jelly every five days, or a piece of apple or banana.

sections.title: Finding and feeding the brood
sections.text: Have the larval containers ready before you open the laying box. I found animals throughout the substrate, so I work through the full depth in small portions. The September brood of 46 was the number I recovered from one female at that check. Return feeding larvae to aged hardwood or flake soil, with enough substrate to burrow. Cottonwood is the common name, but oak is also a natural food. Reyes-Castillo and colleagues found late-stage grubs in a decaying oak stump in Chihuahua.

sections.title: Pupation and emergence
sections.text:
As a grub matures, check the sides and base of its enclosure before loosening the substrate. The Mexican study followed third instars through the rest of development. They pupated in wood debris. Five individuals took five to eight days to pass from prepupa to pupa, and seven took another 31–35 days from pupa to adult. Some adults spent much of their time below a log even after completing the molt. I wait for my beetles to become active on their own before moving them to a pairing enclosure.
In earlier broods I lost pupae, and some newly emerged adults had enlarged abdomens that extended beyond the wing covers. Those adults later died following infection. In my 2026 brood I kept the substrate drier as larvae began to pupate. Most of the adults emerged without those deformities.

species.name: Lucanus capreolus
species.intro: I found young reddish-brown stag beetle larvae in August and recovered 65 grubs from a single female’s laying enclosure in September. With a brood that size, much of the work is having enough feeding substrate ready once the grubs are big enough to separate.

facts.title: Substrate
facts.text: Aged hardwood sawdust or less-fermented hardwood flake soil

facts.title: Adult diet
facts.text: Beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana

sections.title: Choosing adults and setting the pair
sections.text:
Look for the contrasting pale and dark areas on the femora, the long segment of each leg nearest the body. These patches distinguish the adults from the similar smooth stag beetle, which has uniformly dark femora. I often see fungal growth on wild reddish-brown stags, so I look over the body and legs when choosing a pair. I offer beetle jelly every five days once adults are active, with apple or banana as alternatives. A piece of bark gives them a place to grip at the feeding site.
This was the first stag beetle I kept. I have found adults beneath streetlights in Alabama and have observed a pair mating. In my own laying boxes this species has accepted my usual flake soil.

sections.title: Laying substrate and recovering grubs
sections.text: I use aged hardwood sawdust for this species. For a laying box, I recommend less-fermented hardwood flake soil with pieces of decaying hardwood set into it. My flake mix contains sawdust, flour, yeast and a little oatmeal, and I stir the batch over one to two months as it ferments. I prepare the larval containers before taking down the breeding box. Lift each piece of wood over the box, then work through the surrounding material a little at a time so that tiny grubs are easy to see. Give growing larvae a fresh supply of woody substrate as they convert their food into fecal pellets.

sections.title: Pupation and the adult molt
sections.text: Before replacing substrate for a mature grub, look for a cell along the wall or bottom of the container. Leave the chamber intact and wait for the beetle to emerge and become active. I had adults emerging in September. In a later group some newly emerged beetles had abnormal abdomens. I could not establish a cause. I keep that observation separate from the fungal growth I have seen on wild adults.

species.name: Lucanus placidus
species.intro: I recovered 54 larvae from one smooth stag beetle female. The most conspicuous change came much later, when grubs that had seemed stalled for months began making the transition to prepupae. A productive laying box is worth preparing for, and a quiet larval container can reward patience.

facts.title: Substrate
facts.text: Aged hardwood sawdust or less-fermented hardwood flake soil

facts.title: Pupation in my culture
facts.text: Prepupae observed July 26 and a pupa by July 31

sections.title: Adults and the laying box
sections.text:
I have seen this species fly readily in May. The male’s mandibles generally have several small teeth along their inner edge, and both sexes have dark femora. Those characters help distinguish them from the reddish-brown stag beetle. Check for active adults after dusk. I offer beetle jelly every five days, with apple or banana as alternatives. I use aged hardwood sawdust with this species. For a breeding female I recommend a container of less-fermented hardwood flake soil and some decaying hardwood, with bark at the surface for climbing.
One autumn my captive-bred males were active by the end of October, but I had no female ready to pair with them. I check activity in both sexes before planning the next laying box. My females have laid in the same flake soil I normally use for stag beetles.

sections.title: Housing a brood
sections.text: I like to have the rearing containers and a supply of the same woody food ready before inspecting a laying box. My count of 54 is the number of larvae I found from that particular female. Work through the bedding in small portions so newly hatched grubs are easy to spot. As larvae grow, watch the balance of edible wood and fecal pellets. Refresh the feeding material while they are active. Once a mature larva settles in one place and starts pressing the substrate into an oval chamber, leave that section alone.

sections.title: Timing pupation
sections.text: My larvae remained apparently stalled for several months. Then a faulty air conditioner made the room unusually cool for a few days. On July 26 all the stalled larvae had become prepupae, and by July 31 I had a pupa. I did not measure the temperature during that cool spell. For a documented individual timeline, A. A. Girault followed a Virginia grub that became a prepupa around August 1, pupated on August 3 and molted to an adult on October 6. A cell can therefore remain occupied for weeks after the grub has finished feeding.

species.name: Dorcus parallelus
species.intro: I started five antelope stag beetle larvae on prepared hardwood flake soil. All five survived and grew quickly, and by June some were already building pupal cells. That result is the reason I recommend fermented hardwood sawdust for the growing grubs.

facts.title: Development
facts.text: Some larvae had started building pupal cells in June

sections.title: Choosing a breeding pair
sections.text: If you keep eastern North American Dorcus, check the adults before you pair them. Dorcus parallelus resembles Dorcus brevis, and a small male can have short jaws. Look from above at the two rear corners of the pronotum, the shield immediately behind the head. In D. parallelus they sit well forward of the wing covers. In D. brevis the corners approach their bases. A male D. parallelus also has a dense brush of hairs on the inner surface of the hind tibia. I offer active adults beetle jelly every five days. Apple or banana can also be used.

sections.title: Preparing the laying box
sections.text:
I recommend less-fermented hardwood flake soil with pieces of decaying hardwood worked into it. Oak, maple and linden are all recorded as breeding woods in the field. Leave a range of textures, including wood firm enough to remain in one piece when the rest of the substrate is lifted. I found a larva in my breeding enclosure in September. When checking for young grubs, lift the wood over the box and sort the bedding in small portions. Return occupied wood to the enclosure so grubs inside can continue feeding.
In an earlier setup I used fermented oak sawdust with a chunk of rotten wood. I have also housed five females with two males for pairing. When I want an individual brood count, I give each female a separate laying box.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae and recognizing pupation
sections.text: I counted five living grubs in May. At my June check all five larvae in the flake-soil trial were alive, and some were already shaping pupal cells. For a new brood I start with lightly fermented hardwood flake soil. Before loosening spent food, I check the container walls for cells, particularly once the grubs approach full size. When one has settled into a chamber, I leave that part of the container undisturbed while its siblings continue feeding.

species.name: Rutela formosa
species.intro: I have found dozens of Rutela formosa on Key Largo. A mating pair and fresh beetle jelly were easy to provide. The harder part was finding the right place for the female to lay. My early setup with ordinary flake soil produced no brood. I later bred the species with a log resting on the substrate.

facts.title: Adult lifespan
facts.text: About one month in my care

facts.title: Adult food
facts.text: Beetle jelly, renewed every five days

facts.title: Laying material
facts.text: A decayed hardwood log on the surface of the substrate

facts.title: Larval food
facts.text: The interior of the breeding log

sections.title: Feeding and pairing the adults
sections.text: I prepare the breeding enclosure before I introduce the pair because the adults live only about a month. Mine accept beetle jelly, which I renew on my usual five-day schedule. I put it on an accessible part of the surface so I can replace it while leaving the log in position. At Key Largo I have found adults in numbers, yet even an active group in captivity gave me no offspring when I offered only my usual flake soil.

sections.title: What changed when I added a log
sections.text: In 2021, my standard flake-soil setup failed to produce a brood. By May 2022 I had at least four pairs on hand. I keep that count separate from my later breeding results. In my later culture I used the same basic arrangement I use for Dorcus: a breeding log resting on the surface of the substrate. I choose decaying hardwood that still holds together as a log. The solid piece matters throughout the brood’s development. Once the female has had access to it, I leave it in the enclosure, even if I cannot see any young at the surface.

sections.title: Following larvae inside the wood
sections.text: My grubs fed through the log and hollowed it from within. I never saw them leave it, even in captivity. I would keep occupied wood intact when refreshing the surrounding material. An empty-looking layer of flake soil tells me very little about what is happening inside the log. In Florida, larvae, pupae and adults have also been found in the decayed heartwood of Bursera and Metopium logs. That field observation fits the way my grubs used the wood.

sections.title: Adults in the field and in culture
sections.text: The striped adult on bark is from my collection in September 2025. The Florida field photograph in the gallery is from December 2024. It shows the markings in natural light and gives a sense of the beetle’s size on a hand. I keep these field dates separate from the time an adult spends active in a breeding box.

species.name: Odontotaenius floridanus
species.intro: I have bred the Florida bess beetle through three broods without giving my group a winter cooling period. Finding the beetles took considerably longer than getting them to breed. Between us, Alan and I spent at least eight days in the field over roughly six trips before we found them.

facts.title: Rearing material
facts.text: Breeding logs buried in homemade flake soil

facts.title: Winter treatment
facts.text: No deliberate cooling period in this culture

sections.title: Preparing the wood
sections.text: I buried breeding logs in my homemade flake soil. This was the setup in which I saw the first brood in March 2025. I keep the wood in one piece so the adults can establish galleries and the young have somewhere to feed alongside them. When starting another enclosure, I would use softened hardwood with enough structure to keep those tunnels intact. I keep the wood and the material the adults have worked together when checking the culture.

sections.title: Recognizing a brood
sections.text: I found a newly hatched first instar on April 14, 2025, and photographed a pupa on May 16. By June 7 the second brood was building pupal cells against the enclosure wall. I generally found around four larvae per brood. The April and May dates are separate checks rather than a measured developmental interval for one animal. In a bess beetle enclosure the parents and young share the wood, so I leave the family together. When I check on them, I look along an existing opening and preserve the chewed material around the gallery. For counting broods I use positive sightings of young. The adults can remain alive for a long time without producing offspring.

sections.title: Keeping the culture going
sections.text: By September 2025 the colony had given me a third brood. I had given it no deliberate winter cooling period between broods. I keep wood available whenever the beetles have hollowed out much of the original piece, and I would place fresh wood alongside the occupied material. In April 2026 my first-generation adults were still alive, although I had yet to see them start a brood of their own. My result with this Florida species is quite different from the compacted-sawdust setup I tried with Odontotaenius disjunctus, in which the adults lived but I recovered no young.

species.name: Stenodontes exsertus
species.intro: The Puerto Rican giant longhorn is a larger, redder relative of Stenodontes chevrolati. The adults I have seen have long, curved mandibles with a smooth inner edge. The species occurs on Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. My breeding notes come from Puerto Rican stock, and keeping the laying medium almost dry made a real difference to the eggs.

facts.title: Laying setup
facts.text: About 2 inches (5 cm) of nearly dry sawdust, with bark on top

sections.title: A shallow, dry laying bed
sections.text: I put about 2 inches (5 cm) of sawdust in the breeding container and lay pieces of bark on the surface. The sawdust I use is very nearly bone dry. In a damp laying bed the eggs have molded and rotted, and young larvae have also rotted. For that reason I avoid using moist flake soil or white-rotten wood as the laying bed for my Puerto Rican stock. The bark gives the adult cover without having to wet the whole bed.

sections.title: Moving the young larvae
sections.text: I can rear the larvae in the same sort of sawdust. By February 23, 2026, I had rehoused 36 of them and was still working through the group. That is a count of the larvae I moved that day. In late March the young larvae I had available measured about 7–10 mm. They are small enough at that stage that it is worth taking the sawdust apart carefully.

sections.title: Results on kinshi
sections.text: I have also used kinshi, wood substrate colonized by a fungus, for the feeding larvae. Most of my S. exsertus were doing well on an oyster-mushroom batch when I checked them in November 2026. I had put Callipogon proletarius larvae on that same batch and lost every one of them. The contrast is worth keeping in mind when choosing a fungus for longhorn larvae. A substrate that supports a feeding larva also has a different job from the dry bed I give a laying female.

sections.title: Recognizing the stock in the field
sections.text: I have reared unidentified longhorn larvae from fallen logs in Puerto Rico. The ones I took from those logs turned out to be Callipogon when they matured. Finding a large larva in a downed log was therefore a poor way for me to identify S. exsertus. A published host record for S. exsertus names Zanthoxylum, the prickly ashes.

species.name: Callipogon proletarius
species.intro: This large Caribbean longhorn has long antennae and a broad head. I photographed an adult in January 2026 and recorded hatching later that month. My clearest result so far concerns the fungus used to rear the larvae. Two kinds of kinshi gave very different outcomes.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: The nominate form is recorded from Puerto Rico

facts.title: Unsuccessful larval substrate
facts.text: All larvae in the oyster-kinshi group died

sections.title: Adults and hatching
sections.text: The January adult shows the heavy build of this longhorn clearly. On January 30 I photographed a small rearing cup when I found that the eggs had hatched. Those two dates show when I saw an adult and when I found young larvae. I did not record when each egg was laid, so I cannot give an incubation time for this group.

sections.title: Choosing kinshi for feeding larvae
sections.text: I kept larvae on two kinds of kinshi, a substrate of wood colonized by a fungus. By early November the larvae in turkey-tail kinshi were growing well. Every larva I kept on oyster-mushroom kinshi had died. Most of my Stenodontes exsertus larvae were doing well in that same oyster batch, which is why I keep a separate substrate record for each longhorn species. For another group of C. proletarius, I would begin with turkey-tail kinshi.

sections.title: What the trial established
sections.text: I followed this group from hatching into the feeding stage. My November check established which of the two substrates had supported growth up to that point. I still have no measured larval period, pupal duration or adult emergence rate from that comparison.

species.name: Eleodes hispilabris
species.intro: I kept this western North American darkling beetle through two captive generations in a single colony bin. I left the eggs and young with the adults. A deep bed of desert sand with a little wood mixed through it gave me a practical way to raise successive generations without searching for individual eggs.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: Western North America, from western Canada south to Arizona and Texas

sections.title: Building the colony enclosure
sections.text: I used a 20-quart bin and filled it about halfway with Exo Terra desert sand. I mixed a small amount of wood into the sand, then set pieces of bark on top. The wood was a minor part of the mixture. The adults lived and laid in this same enclosure.

sections.title: Leaving the eggs in place
sections.text: When I was asked how I found the eggs, my answer was that I left them where the females had laid them. The eggs hatched in the adult enclosure. Substrate moisture was the detail I watched. I kept the sand from drying out completely, while also avoiding soaking it. I did not need separate incubation cups to get the next generation.

sections.title: Feeding the colony
sections.text: I fed the beetles fish flakes and dog food. By August 2025 this arrangement had carried the culture through two generations. I followed the colony as a group, so I cannot attach a clutch size or a precise time from egg to adult to any one female.

species.name: Embaphion muricatum
species.intro: The upturned rim of this beetle’s back is what first caught my eye. I kept pie-dish beetles in December 2021 and had larvae of Embaphion muricatum available by March 2022. In 2024 Alan reared a fresh group to its first adult. The young are slender soil-dwellers, quite unlike the broad, shallow-dished adults.

facts.title: Our stock
facts.text: Larvae in March 2022, new adult in July 2024

facts.title: Successful substrate
facts.text: About 3 in (7.5 cm) of ReptiSoil mixed with excavator clay

facts.title: Pupation site
facts.text: An earthen cell below the surface

sections.title: A substrate that produced an adult
sections.text: Alan’s account from July 2024: I received fresh stock earlier that year and set it up in a gasket-sealed tub. I mixed ReptiSoil with excavator clay and gave the beetles about three inches (7.5 cm) of this mixture. I did not add rotten wood. On July 10 I saw the first adult from that group. This is the setup I would start with for another batch of pie-dish larvae.

sections.title: Starting with adults
sections.text: I would give the adults cover they can walk under and a bed of diggable soil deep enough for the larvae to disappear into it. My Eleodes hispilabris setup offers one way to arrange a darkling enclosure. For pie-dish beetles I would leave a slightly damp area below the surface so a full-grown larva can form a cell that holds its shape. I would keep the feeding area accessible for checks without turning over the whole enclosure.

sections.title: Feeding the larvae
sections.text: Wheat, hulless oats and rye are useful foods to start with. Both adults and larvae accepted seeds in laboratory feeding trials. I would offer a small amount at a recognizable spot and check the grains as well as the soil beneath them. A larva can eat into a seed from below while leaving little sign at the surface.

sections.title: Following pupation
sections.text: Once I have larger larvae, I would leave part of the bed undisturbed and check through the side of the container. The finished cell is fragile, so I would wait for the adult to leave it before moving the beetle. In Kansas both larvae and adults have been found overwintering. My March 2022 larvae establish which stage I had that spring, but the interval after my December account is not a measured egg-to-larva time.

species.name: Thylodrias contractus
species.intro: I started my odd beetle culture with about 30 living larvae that I recovered from a damaged insect collection in February 2026. The beetles were especially common around moths and orthopterans. By mid-March several had matured. Two months later I nearly wrote the culture off before I spotted the tiny larvae of the next generation.

sections.title: Moving the larvae
sections.text: I first look beneath damaged specimens and in the loose debris around them. That was where I could recover living larvae among the remains. For a new colony I would move some of the material on which the larvae have already been feeding to a separate, close-fitting container. I considered crickets as a substitute for the dried insects. The damage I actually observed was to moths and orthopterans in the collection. I keep a live culture well away from pinned specimens.

sections.title: Recognizing adults of both sexes
sections.text: An adult female can look so much like a larva that it is easy to overlook her during a count. Females are wingless throughout adult life. Males have wing covers, but the hind wings underneath vary considerably in size. I look for both forms when checking for maturity, then use the appearance of a new size class of small larvae as evidence of reproduction.

sections.title: When the enclosure looks empty
sections.text: Several larvae had matured during the two weeks before my March 15 check. On May 19, small larvae finally caught my eye in the enclosure. I would keep an apparently quiet container and examine the remaining food under magnification before starting over. A laboratory study found a typical life cycle of 12.8 months, with individuals ranging from about six and a half months to more than 46 months. My February founders were already larvae when I collected them, so their March emergence tells me when the first adults appeared, but not their total age.

species.name: Dermestes marmoratus
species.intro: Of the four or so Dermestes species I had seen by August 2025, this was the largest. My beetles began breeding in their temporary enclosure. I photographed an adult in September. Its mottled wing covers make a good field mark to look for when checking which species has established in a box.

facts.title: Captive result
facts.text: Breeding in the holding enclosure by August 29, 2025

facts.title: Adult size
facts.text: 9–13 mm in the North American identification key

sections.title: Starting a colony
sections.text: I would begin with a small amount of dry animal material and leave the group together. The food history of this species gives me a better starting point than a fruit or jelly feeder. Its published records include carrion and accumulations of dead insects. I would supply a separate piece of dry material to lift when I check the box so I can find young larvae without disturbing the whole group.

sections.title: Checking the holding box
sections.text: My first breeding result came while the group was still in temporary housing. For that reason I check the food, loose debris and sheltered edges before moving the adults into a permanent setup. Small larvae can remain behind when the conspicuous adults have all been transferred. I keep this colony separate from the dry insects in my specimen collection.

sections.title: Recognizing the adults
sections.text: Under good light I look for a marbled pattern of dark and pale hairs on the wing covers. A paler band extends inward from behind each shoulder. Several North American Dermestes are mottled, so I use the identification key when starting with new field material. The September photograph shows the appearance of my own adult.

species.name: Gibbium aequinoctiale
species.intro: My smooth spider beetles were slow to establish. In July 2024, around two years after I remembered starting the culture, I counted roughly 30 adults. I had raised Mezium affine on the same food, and that colony built up much sooner. The two are similar enough in the hand that I like to compare them under magnification.

sections.title: Feeding and checking the colony
sections.text: I used dog food for both of my spider beetle species. With Gibbium I also considered trying oats and artificial pollen. The food I can recommend from my own breeding result is dog food. I would offer it in small pieces that I can lift and inspect, and keep the crumbs in the culture until I have checked them for tiny beetles. A close-fitting lid and fine ventilation are worthwhile with adults this small.

sections.title: Allowing for a slow start
sections.text: By my July 21 check I could see about 30 adults. The culture took roughly three times as long to get established as my Mezium affine. The adults seemed short-lived to me, although I could not tell whether a delay during the egg or larval stage accounted for the slow buildup. I use the two-year figure to describe the history of my colony. It does not represent the developmental time of an individual. I once thought I had lost the culture because I could hardly find adults during the day. A night check showed they were still active.

sections.title: Telling my two cultures apart
sections.text: I check the head and the narrow shield just behind it. Both are smooth in Gibbium, as are the shiny, swollen wing covers. In Mezium affine, the head and shield have conspicuous pale hairs. These are widespread spider beetles associated with stored materials and found in North America. I label each culture before moving food or beetles between containers.

species.name: Mezium affine
species.intro: I bred this small, round spider beetle on dog food. Of the two spider beetles I kept, Mezium affine was the quicker to build into an established colony. Its polished wing covers look much like those of Gibbium aequinoctiale, but a hand lens shows that the front of the body is covered in hairs.

sections.title: Care and feeding
sections.text: I use the same staple food that worked for my Gibbium colony. I would keep small portions of dog food in a secure container and check the food and crumbs together. I use a pale tray for looking through a small sample. Against a light surface it is easier to see the tiny, reddish-brown adults move away from the food. Before replacing the bottom material, I would keep a portion with the established group. In October 2025 I found grain mites in my Mezium culture. Since both can be present in the crumbs, I would check them under magnification before moving material to a fresh box.

sections.title: Following the colony
sections.text: I compare the numbers of adults I can see at successive checks. My Mezium became established substantially sooner than the Gibbium, which took roughly three times as long to build up. That comparison is about the time it took my cultures to become productive. I did not follow a single egg through to adulthood in that comparison.

sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: For a quick comparison, I look immediately behind the head. A coat of pale hairs covers the head and pronotum, while the much larger wing covers have a glossy surface. I check those characters before transferring beetles between cultures. The species occurs in North America and elsewhere in stored animal and plant products, which fits its readiness to use dog food in my care.

species.name: Zopherus nodulosus
species.intro: The Texas ironclads in my enclosure gathered on lichen and fed readily. I keep the black-and-white Texas form, Zopherus nodulosus haldemani. In my latest breeding trial I changed how I arranged the wood, standing spent mushroom logs upright to give the beetles access to the sides as well as the ends.

sections.title: Feeding the adults
sections.text: I offer lichen on its supporting bark so I can see where the beetles have been feeding. In the photograph, several adults are gathered on the same piece. For another group I would keep a feeding surface accessible at the front of the enclosure.

sections.title: The upright-log trial
sections.text: For my November 2026 setup I stacked spent mushroom logs vertically. I wanted to see whether wood already worked by the fungus would support the larvae. I would keep the logs stable while checking the adults and retain any piece that shows signs of tunnelling. Feeding was the result I had confirmed when I photographed the setup. I was still waiting to rear larvae from the wood.

sections.title: Beetle Substrate Guide
sections.subtitle: Lets make this as easy as possible
paragraphs: Here are the very basics: in regards to US native species, Dynastes tityus and granti, Strategus aloeus and antaeus, Gymnetis thula and any Cotinis species, Osmoderma species and Euphoria species can be raised on "Organic Raised Bed Soil" alone! If a larger size is desired, simply mix in raw sawdust! This will be explained in the next slide. But without any mixtures, the organic soil alone will achieve average sized adult beetles!

sections.title: Mixing the Organic Raised Bed Soil
sections.subtitle: Say goodbye to hard to make flake soil!
paragraphs: So if you decide to go down the dark path of ditching flake soil once and for all, but still want that sweet large major male, know that it is still very doable, and easy! Mix in 3/10th of the substrate mass in raw sawdust, you can use any of the hardwood grilling pellets consisting of Oak or Mesquite wood. I personally opt for Mesquite as it is the most affordable option. Make sure the sawdust expands and stir it with the "Organic Raised Bed Soil" throughly. Leave the mixture for two weeks, and stir it whenever you remember to do so (doesn't have to be often). Once the two weeks is up, it is ready for you to add beetles!

A. make sure the organic soil you use do not compose of cow manure. Cow manure contains a bacteria that can cause leg rot with a lot of beetle larvae species and can kill your larvae quickly. That said, most "Organic Raised Bed Soil" purchased from Walmart or Home Depot does not contain cow manure and can be used without issues.
B. This substrate mix is not meant for: any US Lucanid (stag beetles), and any of them Phileurus or Hemiphileurus species.
C. If the intent is to raise large cetoniids (flower beetles), adding a large portion of rotting leaves will also yield desirable results, although raw sawdust works perfectly fine.

sections.title: Making Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: You gotta do it sometime
paragraphs: You really don't have to stress about making flake soil - things ferment in the wild all without human intervention after all. But sometimes, we just gotta speed it up!

sections.title: How to Make Flake Soil
sections.subtitle: Can't be that hard can it?
paragraphs: First up - if you leave raw sawdust by itself in a moist state long enough, certain lucanids will eat it. Yes, you heard me right, the more hardy species will do just fine on aged sawdust. But this might cost you 6 months - a year's time.
So, how do you make flake soil?

Well, you will need ingredients first. 20lbs of hardwood grilling pellets of just about any brand will do the trick for the wood part, but oak and mesquite are your best choices. Then, you need to add 7.5lbs of unbleached flour, and some dry yeast.
The first step is to pour out and expand the pellets with water, and then turn it into sawdust. Warm water works best with this step, but cold will do just fine.

Then you pour the flour into the expanded pellets, along with a table spoon of yeast. You want to mix throughly here, so there isn't huge clumps of flour - an occasional small piece here and there is fine.

The end result should be damp, but not wet. You can check it by squeezing the substrate. It should form a clump and not fall apart when released, all the while having no water come out. If you made it too wet, leave it in somewhere sunny for a few days and stir more often, you will be fine.

Now the waiting game begins. In this stage, you want to mix up the substrate at least once in 2 days (once a day is better). You should notice the substrate heating up, if it does not heat up, simply add more yeast.
It will be about 3 weeks to a month before the soil is ready. Be sure to wait till the substrate is fully cooled down.
Yay, now you have flake soil! The rest of beetle keeping will be a breeze!
